# Afterword: What You Built, and Where Next {.unnumbered .backmatter #sec-afterword}

Near the end of the water analysis, one setting changed in one script, and the officials' report, the council's
slides, the blog post and the dashboard all changed with it, without a number retyped. That moment is
what the book's projects were for. The London guide, the Acme evaluation and the water analysis each
started from plain text and data, became a shelf of documents for different readers, and rebuild with one command. The projects
will date. The method will not, and it fits on a card.

::: {.practice title="Prompt, Check, Publish"}
**Prompt.** Write the rules down before the first request: a short `AGENTS.md` keeps an agent to the
project's scope, data rules and commands across sessions. Then ask for one task at a time, naming the
file, the column and the output, and ending with a check.

**Check.** Compute every number, so that it updates and can be traced to its data. Before a rebuild,
predict what should change; afterwards, check that it did. Say what a result does not show.

**Publish.** Compute once, publish many: one script writes the results, and every output reads them.
Guard the sentences whose words depend on the data, and keep a known-good state, a checkpoint or a
commit, so that being stuck is a short detour.
:::

The water analysis added four habits that travel to any analysis. Follow one case, your own Tunja, through every
step, because aggregates hide what a single place shows. Label each variable for what it measures, as
"utility-supplied" did for the IRCA. Never define groups by the outcome you will compare them on. And
open every reference an agent gives you before you cite it.

The formats were never the goal. Work with data, software and AI applications pays off when its
audience engages with it and acts on it: a manager decides, a council funds a water supply, a
reader tries the method. Quarto, git and a hosting service make that work reproducible, so
others can trust it, act on it and build on it; an agent makes it fast; checking keeps it
right. What stays with you is the judgement no tool
makes: who the work is for, and what would make them read it.

## What you can now do {.unnumbered}

If you worked through Parts II and V, the London guide and the water analysis, you can:

- explain how Quarto turns one plain-text source into many formats, and why a computed number cannot
  drift from its data;
- direct a coding agent safely, with written rules, one task per prompt and a check after each;
- build and publish a site from data for several readers, as you did for London and for the water
  analysis;
- read an agent's change with `git diff` before you keep it, and undo one with `git restore`;
- predict which outputs a changed input or setting updates, rebuild, and explain the result;
- say which edition of this book shows each interactive figure, and why.

If you also worked through Parts III and IV, the Acme evaluation, you can:

- compute results once and have every document read them, with tests, guards and the render
  each catching what the others miss;
- ask for slides, a branded site and a white paper by name, and check each against what makes
  it work;
- make one document for many values, and render and check every one with a script;
- have every pull request rebuilt by CI, so that a guard the results no longer support turns it
  red.

If one of these is shaky, go back to that part's exercises, starting from a known-good state in
@sec-checkpoints.

## Projects of your own {.unnumbered #sec-own-projects}

The London guide, the Acme evaluation and the water analysis were practice. The five projects here are the kind of
document you already make, or will soon be asked for, built the book's way. Each ends with the
same proof, a rebuild from a fresh copy, so you know that someone else could make it too.

Inside each project the order is the one the book followed. Start with one output for one
reader; make it compute, so that no number is typed; then add formats. The second format is where
the approach starts to repay the setup; the first change to the data is where it pays for itself.

::: {.practice title="Which project first?"}
Choose the one with a real reader and a date: a brief your manager reads on the first Monday, a
supplement due with a resubmission, a report due in three weeks, an update investors expect on
the 5th, a design review next week. Then check that you are allowed
to use its data with an agent ([below](#sec-project-start)). If two qualify, start with the smaller. Finish one
project, fresh clone included, before you start another; the second goes faster.
:::

### Start every project the same way {.unnumbered #sec-project-start}

The design document is the exception: it lives in a repository you already have, so skip this
setup and start on a branch there, as in @sec-fast-path. For the others, make the project folder
and go into it (@sec-first-files): for the brief, `mkdir ~/metrics-brief`
then `cd ~/metrics-brief`. Make a `data/` folder inside it (`mkdir data`) and copy your files in,
unchanged; Finder or File Explorer will do. Start the history with `git init -b main` and
commit the data, `git add data` then `git commit -m "Data, as exported"` (@sec-first-git).
Then hand the agent the setup, with rules written before the first
request (@sec-agents-md). This prompt and the ones below are examples: change the file and
column names to yours.

::: {.prompt}
```default
Set up this folder for a Quarto report with `uv`: run `uv init --bare`, then `uv add ipykernel nbclient nbformat pyyaml pandas matplotlib`. Write AGENTS.md: files in data/ are inputs, never edit them; every number comes from data/ through code; run quarto through `uv run`. Write a .gitignore for .venv/, .quarto/ and the rendered outputs. Show me `git status`.
```
:::

It writes `AGENTS.md`, `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock` and `.gitignore`; the layouts below show the
rest. New files appear in `git status` as untracked, not in `git diff`, so open and read them,
then commit them yourself. From then on, read each change with `git diff` (@sec-first-agent) and
commit after every prompt whose result you checked, so that a bad turn is one `git restore` away.

::: {.practice title="Keep private data private"}
What an agent reads is sent to the model on its vendor's servers (@sec-model-harness). Before a
confidential file meets an agent, read your organisation's AI and data policy; if the agent is
not approved for the data, build the project on a made-up file with the same columns, labelled as
such, and render the real one yourself. @sec-at-work-confidential has the habits in full, and
what each vendor's plan does with what it is sent.
:::

### An internal metrics brief {.unnumbered #sec-project-metrics}

**Who it is for.** Anyone who sends the same figures every month: an analyst, an operations
lead, a manager. Each month you export a CSV from your own tool (a CRM, a ticketing system, a
finance package) and turn it into a one-page brief, as a web page and a Word file. **Start with:**

```text
metrics-brief/
├── AGENTS.md
├── data/
│   ├── 2026-09.csv   each month's export, saved unchanged
│   └── 2026-10.csv
├── brief.qmd         the agent writes it
├── pyproject.toml
└── uv.lock
```

**You build** `brief.html` and `brief.docx`. The first prompt makes one output that computes:

::: {.prompt}
```default
Write brief.qmd with formats html and docx. Read the newest file in data/ (files are named YYYY-MM.csv) and state its month, its number of rows and the total of `amount`, each as inline code. Render, and tell me which file it read.
```
:::

Then the comparison a reader acts on:

::: {.prompt}
```default
In brief.qmd, add a table of total `amount` by `region` for the newest month and the one before, with the change, and a bar chart of the change with a caption and alt text. Render both formats; check that the table's total equals the sentence's.
```
:::

An export can change shape when someone renames a column, so make the brief say so instead of
printing nonsense, and let code choose the words of the one sentence that depends on the data:

::: {.prompt}
```default
Make brief.qmd stop with an error naming the column if the newest export lacks `date`, `region` or `amount`. Test it on a renamed copy in a temporary folder, then delete the copy and render again.
```
:::

::: {.prompt}
```default
Add a sentence saying whether the total rose or fell since the month before, its wording chosen by code from the two totals. Render, and show me the sentence.
```
:::

**Checks only you can do.** Open the export in its own tool and compare one region's total with
the brief's. Open the Word file: does it fit one page? Show it to one reader and ask what they
would do differently after reading it; if the answer is "nothing", the brief needs a different
question, not more charts.

**The rebuild test is next month's file.** When it arrives, save it in `data/`, predict
which numbers will change, render, and compare (@sec-first-change). To rehearse now, remove the
newest export (`rm data/2026-10.csv`), predict, render, then bring it back with
`git restore data/2026-10.csv`.

::: done
next month's export rebuilds both formats with no other edit, one region's total matches the
tool's, and [the fresh-clone test](#sec-fresh-clone) gives the same brief.
:::

### A reproducible research supplement {.unnumbered #sec-project-supplement}

**Who it is for.** Researchers with a paper in progress. The supplement holds the paper's figures and
tables, each computed from the data, with captions, alt text and citations, as a web page and a
PDF that reviewers can open and you can rebuild after every revision. **Start with:**

```text
paper-supplement/
├── AGENTS.md
├── data/
│   ├── README.md        each file's source, licence and date
│   └── measurements.csv your data, unchanged
├── references.bib     the agent writes it
├── supplement.qmd     the agent writes it
├── pyproject.toml
└── uv.lock
```

**You build** `supplement.html` and `supplement.pdf`, the PDF made with Typst as in @sec-formats.

::: {.prompt}
```default
Write supplement.qmd with formats html and typst. Add Table S1 from data/measurements.csv: n, mean and standard deviation of `value` by `group`, with a caption. Render both; check that the n values add up to the file's rows.
```
:::

::: {.prompt}
```default
Add Figure S1, `value` by `group` as a box plot, with a caption and alt text that says what the figure shows, not only what it is (`fig-cap`, `fig-alt`). Render both formats; check that the figure and caption appear in the PDF.
```
:::

::: {.prompt}
```default
Add a Data section citing each source in data/README.md, from a new references.bib set as the `bibliography`. List every DOI and URL you used so that I can open each one; cite nothing you could not find.
```
:::

::: {.prompt}
```default
Add an "AI use" section naming the agent and its version and the tasks it did here, with a TODO where I will list the checks I made. Render, and show me the section.
```
:::

The last prompt follows @sec-ai-policy: the tool is never an author, you are responsible for
what it produced, and you say how you used it. The checks are yours to write, because only you
made them.

**Checks only you can do.** Compare every number in the paper's text with the supplement's.
Open every reference, since an agent can produce a plausible one that does not exist
(@sec-water-dashboard), and read the sentence that cites it. Confirm that you may share the
data: consent, ethics approval and data agreements decide, not the agent. Read the journal's rules on supplementary material and on AI use.

::: done
every figure and table in both formats comes from a cell and has a caption and alt text, every
citation opens to the work it names, the AI-use statement names the tool, the tasks and your
checks, and [the fresh-clone test](#sec-fresh-clone) gives the same supplement.
:::

### A coursework report {.unnumbered #sec-project-coursework}

**Who it is for.** Students with an assignment that involves data. **You build** `report.pdf`
and hand it in with the source, so that a marker can rebuild it and see that every number came
from the data. **Start with:**

```text
coursework/
├── AGENTS.md
├── data/survey.csv   the data the assignment gives you, unchanged
├── README.md         how to rebuild it (the agent writes it)
├── report.qmd        the agent writes it
├── pyproject.toml
└── uv.lock
```

Coursework has a rule the other projects lack: the work being marked must be yours. Start
with the course's AI policy, before any other prompt.

::: {.prompt}
```default
Add to AGENTS.md the rules from my course's AI policy, pasted below, and that data/survey.csv must never be edited. Then list, one line each, what you may and may not do for me under them.
```
:::

::: {.prompt}
```default
Write report.qmd with format typst and the sections the assignment brief asks for (pasted below), and one inline-code sentence giving the number of responses in data/survey.csv. Render report.pdf; tell me how you checked the number.
```
:::

::: {.prompt}
```default
Write README.md: what the project is, and how to rebuild report.pdf from a fresh copy (install uv and Quarto, then `uv run quarto render report.qmd`). Then add an AI-use statement at the end of report.qmd in the form my course asks for. Render, and show me both.
```
:::

If the policy forbids an agent for assessed work, build the project by hand, as in
@sec-first-report: everything here except the prompts still applies.

**Checks only you can do.** Read the policy yourself, and ask the course leader when it is
unclear; the agent's summary of it is not permission. Make sure you can explain every line of
code and every sentence, since a marker may ask. Check the brief's length and format rules
against the PDF. Hand in the source the way the course asks; for a zip of exactly what you
committed (no `.venv/`, no rendered files), run `git archive -o coursework-source.zip HEAD`.

::: done
`report.pdf` answers the brief, the AI-use statement matches both what you did and what the
policy allows, and [the fresh-clone test](#sec-fresh-clone), run by following your own
`README.md`, gives the same PDF.
:::

### A monthly investor update {.unnumbered #sec-project-investor}

**Who it is for.** A founder or an early team who writes to investors every month, as Acme did
in @sec-parameters, but from your own figures. Your figures, not a model's: customers, revenue,
burn and cash, kept in a spreadsheet you export as CSV, and a few lines in your own words on
what happened and what you need. **Start with:**

```text
investor-update/
├── AGENTS.md
├── data/metrics.csv   one row a month: month, customers, mrr, burn, cash
├── notes/
│   └── 2026-10.md     your highlights and asks, in your words, no numbers
├── update.qmd         the agent writes it
├── pyproject.toml
└── uv.lock
```

Investors' figures are confidential: keep the repository private, and send the PDF, not a
link to a page. **You build** `update.pdf` and `update.docx` for any month.

::: {.prompt}
```default
Write update.qmd, a monthly investor update with formats typst and docx, parameterised by `month` (a cell tagged `parameters` whose default is "latest", meaning the last month in data/metrics.csv). Show that month's `customers`, `mrr` and `cash`, each as inline code, and runway in months as `cash` divided by `burn`, with a note saying how it is computed. Add papermill with `uv add papermill`, render it for the month before the latest with `-P`, and tell me which month it shows.
```
:::

::: {.prompt}
```default
Add each figure's change from the month before, its wording (up, down or unchanged) chosen by code from the figures as printed, and make the render stop with a message listing the valid months if `month` is not in the data. Test it with a month that is not there.
```
:::

::: {.prompt}
```default
Below the figures, include notes/<month>.md, my own words on highlights and asks, and stop with a clear message if that month's notes file is missing. Render the latest month in both formats, and show me the notes as they appear in the PDF.
```
:::

In the test run, these prompts worked as written, on a made-up company. Three things they do not
settle are yours. **Runway** here is cash divided by burn; if your investors expect net burn,
burn less revenue, say so in the prompt and in the note. **Every render overwrites the last**:
`update.pdf` is whichever month you rendered most recently, and a render that fails leaves the
previous month's files in place, so check the month printed in the PDF before you send it, or
name each file by its month with `-M output-file:update-2026-10`, as @sec-params-all does. And
the first month in the data has no month before it; the test run's agent wrote "no earlier month
to compare with", and yours should say something, not stop.

**Checks only you can do.** Compare cash with the bank statement and revenue with your billing
tool, every month. Read the notes as an investor would: an ask without a number or a date is
not an ask. Show the update to a co-founder before it goes out.

**The rebuild test is next month.** Add the row and the notes file, render with no `-P`, and
check that the default found the new month.

::: done
the update for any month in the data renders in both formats with that month's figures and
notes, a month that is not in the data stops the render with the valid list, and
[the fresh-clone test](#sec-fresh-clone) gives the same PDF.
:::

### A design document with live numbers {.unnumbered #sec-project-rfc}

**Who it is for.** An engineer proposing a change to a codebase: a design document, or RFC,
whose case rests on measurements and on what the code allows. The data is not a dataset but the
code itself: a benchmark you run, and settings read from the source, so the document cannot
quote a timing nobody measured or list an option the code no longer has. The example below
compares two ways of counting words in a small package, `textstats`; change the names to your
repository's. **Start with** your repository, on a branch, with Quarto's packages added as in
@sec-fast-path:

```text
your-repository/
├── src/textstats/
│   ├── core.py        the code the proposal changes
│   └── config.py      its settings
└── rfc/
    ├── bench.py       the agent writes it
    ├── results.json   bench.py writes it; commit it
    └── rfc.qmd        the agent writes it
```

::: {.prompt}
```default
Write rfc/bench.py: time `count_words_loop` against `count_words_counter` from src/textstats/core.py on texts of three sizes, five repeats each, and write rfc/results.json with each one's median time and range, the Python version, the machine and the date it ran. Run it, and show me the medians.
```
:::

::: {.prompt}
```default
Write rfc/rfc.qmd, a design document in html and typst with sections Context, Proposal, Measurements, Alternatives and Decision. Measurements reads rfc/results.json for a table and a chart with alt text, says what machine and Python it was measured on, and chooses the word faster or slower by code, with a guard. Leave the other sections as a heading and one line saying what goes there. Render it, and show me the sentence with that word.
```
:::

::: {.prompt}
```default
Add a table of the settings in src/textstats/config.py, read from the code at render time (each name, default and description), so the document cannot list a setting the code no longer has. Render, and tell me how you read them.
```
:::

**You build** `rfc/rfc.html` and `rfc/rfc.pdf`; the prose of Context, Proposal, Alternatives
and Decision is yours. From the test run: Quarto runs the document's code from its own folder,
`rfc/`, so every path in it is relative to `rfc/`: the document reads `results.json`, not
`rfc/results.json`, and reaches the code as `../src/textstats/config.py` or, better, by importing
the package, as the test run's agent did. An agent that copies the prompt's paths into the code
gets "file not found". The rendered files land in `rfc/` too: add them to
`.gitignore`. And alt text cannot be computed in a Python document's cell options (`!expr` is
for R's knitr only); write alt text that describes the chart without its numbers, and let the
table carry them.

**Checks only you can do.** Check the machine's name in `results.json`: on a Mac, Python's
`platform.processor()` says only "arm", and the test run's agent had to ask the system for the
chip's name. Run the benchmark twice. In the test run, the faster function stayed
faster, but medians moved by up to about six per cent between runs, more than five repeats'
range suggested: report the direction and the ratio, not the third decimal place, and say on
what machine it ran. Commit `results.json` with the document, so a reviewer reads the numbers
you measured; re-run it when the code changes. Then ask a reviewer whether the Alternatives
section names the option they would have proposed.

**The rebuild test is the code.** Add a setting to `config.py` and render: the table shows it.
Remove it again.

::: done
the measurements and settings tables come from `results.json` and the code at render time, the
word faster or slower is chosen by code and guarded, and [the fresh-clone test](#sec-fresh-clone)
gives the same document.
:::

### The fresh-clone test {.unnumbered #sec-fresh-clone}

The last check of every project is the one a colleague, a reviewer or a marker will make:
rebuild it from what you committed, on a clean copy. Anything that lived only on your machine, a
file never committed or a step done by hand, shows up here instead of in their inbox.

1. In the project folder, run `git status`. If it lists anything, commit it (@sec-first-git)
   until it says `nothing to commit, working tree clean`.
2. Clone the project into a new folder and render it there. For the brief:

   ```bash
   git clone ~/metrics-brief ~/metrics-brief-check
   cd ~/metrics-brief-check
   uv run quarto render brief.qmd
   ```

   The clone has no `.venv/` and no outputs, because `.gitignore` kept them out of the history,
   so the first render builds the environment again, as in @sec-first-render. A local clone
   copies between folders on your own computer; nothing is uploaded. For the other projects,
   use their folder and file names.
3. Open each output from both folders side by side and compare every number.

A failed render or a different number is a finding, not a failure: commit the missing file, or
turn the manual step into code, and clone again. When the two agree, delete the check folder; it
is only a copy.

Agents, models and Quarto's options will keep changing, and some details in this book with them.
The loop does not. Prompt for one thing. Check it against the data. Publish only what you checked, from
one source, as often as the data change.

## Where next {.unnumbered}

- Quarto's [Guide](https://quarto.org/docs/guide/) covers everything this book used and much it did not:
  books like this one, manuscripts, interactive documents and more output formats (checked 2026-10-30).
- [Dashboards](https://quarto.org/docs/dashboards/), [Typst](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/typst.html)
  and [publishing to GitHub Pages](https://quarto.org/docs/publishing/github-pages.html) are the official
  references for the three areas readers usually extend first (checked 2026-10-30).
- For the causal questions the water analysis left open, Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins,
  [*Causal Inference: What If*](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook) (Boca Raton: Chapman & Hall/CRC,
  2020; free online), on confounding and the designs that can answer them (checked 2026-11-12).
- Quarto's [Citations](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/citations.html) page, and its
  [Manuscripts](https://quarto.org/docs/manuscripts/), projects that write a scholarly article in
  several formats and publish it as a website, take the research supplement further (checked
  2026-11-17).
- In this book: @sec-cheatsheet for the commands, @sec-troubleshooting when a render fails, and
  @sec-checkpoints for every known-good state.
- The workshop's [slides](https://project-delphi.github.io/quarto-workshop/) are online, and its examples and checkpoints are in
  its [GitHub repository](https://github.com/project-delphi/quarto-workshop).
